newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian workers in anti-government "liars march".
newsitem.headline: Belgian workers in anti-government "liars march".

text.p: Thousands of Belgian workers took to the streets of regional capital Namur on Saturday to protest at what they said were politicians' lies and double-speak on jobs.

Wearing long false noses and led by a "lie detector", the protesters, dressed in traditional red and green union colours and waving banners, were due to march past the seat of the Walloon government, the focus of their anger and a possible flashpoint.

The march was led by employees of bankrupt steel maker Forges de Clabecq, which folded in January when the government -- under pressure from the European Commission -- baulked at a request from administrators for fresh aid.
A banner carried by workers' wives accused the government of having abandoned the company. Another said: "European Union (equals) capitalism, social exclusion and slavery".

Many retailers closed for the day, fearful of a repeat of events last year when Clabecq workers and police fought a running battle through the streets of the city. In Brussels on Friday, a jobs protest also turned violent.

Clabecq workers also clashed with riot police last month when they tried to block the Paris-Brussels motorway using bulldozers. Twenty five people were injured, one seriously, and several police vehicles, including water cannon, were damaged.
Police said their presence would remain low-key, unless the workers sought to break through a cordon thrown up around the government quarter.

However, some shop workers said they had closed to join in the protest out of sympathy for the workers' plight. "If there are no jobs, there's no purchasing power and no economy. Zero," one shop owner told RTBF television on Friday.
"I want work for my daddy," said a sign carried by a child.
The Clabecq workers were joined by delegations from Renault Belgium, Volkswagen, Sabena, Cockerill Sambre and Caterpillar Belgium.

More than 3,000 Renault Belgium workers are fighting a decision by the French company to close their factory in July. Staff at airline Sabena, steel maker Cockerill and mechanical digger maker Caterpillar are also facing redundancies or early retirement because of restructuring plans.
"This is not a demonstration for Clabecq but one for jobs," Clabecq union leader Roberto D'Orazio told Reuters.
One banner called for a general strike in Belgium to protest against the country's 13 percent unemployment rate. "500,000 jobless. How did we get here?" another placard said.
However, in what was perhaps a sign that the protests are beginning to wane, police estimated that only 8,000 people had turned up for Saturday's demonstration. The organisers had hoped for 100,000.

The Namur demonstration was the fifth major jobs march in Belgium in two months. A march in Brussels on March 16 led by Renault unions attracted more than 50,000 workers from across Europe. About 40,000 mainly Belgian workers also took part in a march in Tubize, Clabecq's home town, on February 2.
